G-STAR: Group-Scaled Token Capacity for Deeply Compressed Autoregressive Generation

Xu Huang1,2∗  Ye Huang1∗  Xiaotong Li2†‡  Zhengrong Yue2,3  Jialv Zou2,4  Minhao Jing2
Haodong Li2,5  Wenhao Yan2,6  Yaxin Luo2,7  Duomin Wang1  Daquan Zhou1‡ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Discrete autoregressive models offer a scalable framework for image generation. However, they face a fundamental trade-off: long token sequences preserve representation quality but slow generation, while aggressive spatial compression reduces representation capacity. Based on product quantization, we show that, under a fixed nominal information budget, group size should scale quadratically with the per-axis spatial compression factor. Building on this principle, we propose GSTAR, a spatial–group co-scaling framework that enables 32×32\times and even effective 64×64\times compression while preserving strong reconstruction, understanding, and generation performance. Since larger groups introduce intra-group dependencies that must be modeled efficiently, we analyze their impact on inference latency and generation quality and introduce a semi-autoregressive decoder that combines parallel feature computation with lightweight causal modeling. With these designs, our highly compressed models perform competitively with leading models across five representative text-to-image benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench). At 1024×10241024\times 1024 resolution, our model delivers a 20×20\times speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models, generating each image in 2.5 seconds on a single NVIDIA H200. Together, these results show that highly compressed discrete representations can enable high-quality autoregressive generation at low latency.

1 Introduction

Discrete visual tokenization provides a natural interface between image generation and autoregressive sequence modeling. By representing images as sequences of discrete symbols, visual generation can be formulated using the same next-token prediction paradigm that has driven the success of large language models [16, 46]. This formulation has also shown promise for unifying visual generation and multimodal understanding within a single autoregressive architecture [36, 60].

Despite its conceptual simplicity and scalability, discrete visual autoregressive modeling faces two fundamental limitations. First, mapping continuous visual features to a finite codebook introduces quantization error, which can discard fine-grained details and degrade reconstruction fidelity [49, 16]. The same discretization can also remove semantically relevant cues that are important for visual understanding and language alignment, reducing the informativeness of the resulting discrete representation [36, 15, 60]. Second, discrete autoregressive models generate visual tokens sequentially, making inference latency grow with sequence length [46, 51, 1, 60]. This bottleneck is amplified at high resolutions, where the number of tokens grows quadratically with image side length, widening the latency gap with diffusion models that update all spatial positions in parallel at each denoising step [22, 43].

Increasing the spatial compression rate offers a direct way to reduce the number of global autoregressive steps. However, aggressive spatial compression forces each spatial token to encode more information [8, 9], exacerbating the information loss introduced by discrete quantization [49, 16]. To mitigate this loss, we adopt multi-codebook quantization (MCQ) [28, 54, 36], which represents each spatial token with multiple discrete codes and thereby expands its representation capacity. More importantly, MCQ admits a useful scaling property: as detailed in Section 4.2, jointly scaling the spatial compression rate and the number of codes per token can preserve the total nominal information budget while reducing the number of global autoregressive steps. We systematically study how code scaling affects reconstruction, generation, and semantic representation, and find that it enables high-compression tokenizers at 32×32\times and even 64×64\times—well beyond the common 16×16\times setting—while retaining high fidelity and providing an efficient interface for downstream generation.

Multi-codebook quantization requires each global autoregressive step to predict a group of codes. RQ-Transformer-style causal depth decoders model their dependencies, but their latency grows linearly with group size and can dominate the global backbone under aggressive compression [28]. Parallel and masked-token predictors remove this serial cost [4, 51, 40, 31, 5], yet sample the codes independently and may combine incompatible modes—a failure known as multi-modal collision [12]. We therefore introduce a lightweight semi-autoregressive depth decoder: most layers run in parallel, while only the final layer retains a causal path for intra-group conditioning. This keeps group-scaling overhead nearly flat without sacrificing generation quality.

We evaluate our approach on large-scale text-to-image generation using five representative benchmarks: GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench. Our models perform competitively with leading systems across these benchmarks while supporting spatial compression ratios from 32×32\times to 64×64\times. Controlled studies further examine how group scaling affects reconstruction fidelity, generation quality, and semantic representation, and compare the quality–latency trade-off among causal, parallel, and semi-autoregressive intra-group decoders. At 1024×10241024\times 1024 resolution, our model delivers a 20×20\times speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models and generates each image in 2.5 seconds on a single NVIDIA H200.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We systematically study how scaling the group size affects reconstruction, generation, and semantic understanding under 32×32\times and 64×64\times spatial compression, showing that scaling the per-step capacity preserves strong representation quality with a short global sequence.

  • •

    We propose a lightweight semi-autoregressive depth decoder for efficiently modeling intra-group dependencies, together with an optimized inference implementation. Our system generates a 1024×10241024\times 1024 image in 2.5 seconds on a single NVIDIA H200.

  • •

    We further validate the effectiveness of our approach at 32×32\times and even effective 64×64\times spatial compression by training two models, GSTAR-Pro-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B, respectively, in a large-scale text-to-image setting. Our models achieve performance competitive with leading models across Qwen-Image-Bench, PRISM, DPG-Bench, GenEval, and LongText-Bench, while our approach delivers a 20×20\times inference speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models.

2 Related Work

2.1 Discrete Image Generation

Discrete generators learn distributions over quantized visual tokens [49, 16, 46]. Recent advances include next-scale prediction in VAR, Infinity, and NextFlow [47, 21, 60], randomized generation orders in RAR and RandAR [57, 41], and parallel decoding in PAR and BitDance [51, 1]. Janus-Pro and Emu3.5 scale discrete generation within unified multimodal systems [11, 13]; UniAR further combines a shared visual tokenizer with parallel bitwise prediction [42]. GLM-Image pairs autoregressive visual-token prediction with a diffusion image decoder [59].

Representation capacity is another key axis. RQ-Transformer, MAGVIT-v2, GSQ, UniTok, and WeTok explore residual, binary, or grouped quantization [28, 56, 50, 36, 63], while BAR and BitDance model large binary token spaces with masked-bit and diffusion heads, respectively [58, 1]. Building on these advances, we study spatial–group co-scaling at 32×32\times and effective 64×64\times compression, jointly examining reconstruction, semantic representation, and the trade-off of group decoding.

2.2 Discrete Diffusion for Accelerated Generation

MaskGIT and Muse accelerate image generation through iterative parallel unmasking [4, 3]. Show-o combines discrete diffusion with autoregressive language modeling [53], while Emu3.5 adapts pretrained autoregressive models to parallel image-token prediction via DiDA [13]. NVIDIA’s Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Image advances this direction with token editing and grouped cross-entropy for large-vocabulary image synthesis [31].

For speculative language decoding, DFlash uses block-diffusion drafting [5], whereas DSpark combines a parallel backbone with a lightweight sequential module to model intra-block dependencies [12]. Inspired by these approaches, we accelerate intra-group code generation by computing representations for all group slots in parallel, while using a lightweight single-layer causal Transformer to model dependencies among codes.

3 Preliminaries

Multi-codebook quantization.

Multi-codebook quantization (MCQ) represents each spatial token with multiple discrete codes. We instantiate MCQ with product quantization (PQ), implemented as group-wise quantization, for its simplicity and favorable scaling: increasing the number of groups consistently improves reconstruction fidelity (Sec. 5.2.1) [26, 50, 36, 63]. Specifically, PQ partitions the projected feature 𝐳t∈ℝC\mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} into GqG_{q} disjoint channel groups and quantizes each group independently:

kt(g)=arg⁡mink∈[K]⁡‖𝐳t(g)−𝐞k(g)‖22,𝐳^t=Concatg=1Gq​𝐞kt(g)(g).k_{t}^{(g)}=\arg\min_{k\in[K]}\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}^{(g)}-\mathbf{e}_{k}^{(g)}\right\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=\operatorname{Concat}_{g=1}^{G_{q}}\mathbf{e}_{k_{t}^{(g)}}^{(g)}. (1)

The resulting code tuple provides up to KGqK^{G_{q}} configurations per spatial position without increasing the spatial sequence length.

Depth transformer.

RQ-Transformer separates the generation of residual codes into a global spatial transformer and a local depth transformer [28]. The global transformer summarizes preceding spatial units into a context vector, while the depth transformer models the dependencies among the codes assigned to the current unit. We adopt this spatial–depth decomposition for grouped rather than residual codes; the alternative depth-modeling strategies are detailed in Sec. 4.3.

4 Method

Our framework combines a deeply compressed discrete tokenizer with a hierarchical autoregressive generator. We use group scaling to increase the capacity of each spatial token and develop a spatial–group co-scaling principle that preserves the nominal information budget while shortening the global sequence. Building on the native 32×32\times tokenizer, we instantiate this principle through lossless spatial packing to construct an effective 64×64\times tokenizer. A lightweight semi-autoregressive depth decoder then efficiently models the correlated codes within each global step.

4.1 Deeply Compressed Tokenizer for Efficient Generation

We train a discrete tokenizer that maps an image 𝐱\mathbf{x} to a compact grid of group-wise codes and reconstructs it as 𝐱^\hat{\mathbf{x}}, as illustrated in Fig. 2(a). Following recent visual autoencoders and tokenizers built on pretrained semantic encoders [55, 15, 37, 61, 24], we initialize the encoder of our 32×32\times tokenizer from Qwen-ViT [2]. The tokenizer is optimized with standard reconstruction and vector-quantization objectives. To preserve the semantic structure of the pretrained representation after quantization, we additionally align the quantized features with the corresponding Qwen-ViT features. Following Scale-RAE for text-to-image generation [48], we further employ a Gram loss [18] to match second-order feature correlations between the input and its reconstruction. The overall training objective is

ℒtok=ℒrec+λvq​ℒvq+λsem​ℒsem+λgram​ℒgram+λcommit​ℒcommit.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{vq}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vq}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sem}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{gram}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gram}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{commit}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{commit}}. (2)

Here ℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} collects the standard pixel, perceptual, and adversarial reconstruction terms, ℒvq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vq}} is the quantization objective, and ℒsem\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}} is the semantic alignment objective. The commitment loss ℒcommit\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{commit}} encourages encoder features to remain close to their assigned codebook embeddings.

4.2 Scaling the Group Size

Group-wise quantization provides a direct way to increase the discrete capacity assigned to each spatial token without lengthening the global sequence. This is particularly useful under aggressive spatial compression, where each remaining position must preserve more visual information. Let’s denote the effective per-axis spatial compression factor and GG the number of codes generated at each global position. For the native 32×32\times tokenizer, G=GqG=G_{q}, the number of quantization groups. With a fixed codebook size KK, the relationships illustrated in Fig. 2(b) are

Nglobal​(s)\displaystyle N_{\mathrm{global}}(s) =H​Ws2,Cstep(G,K)=Glog2K,\displaystyle=\tfrac{HW}{s^{2}},\quad C_{\mathrm{step}}(G,K)=G\log_{2}K, (3)
Btotal​(s,G,K)\displaystyle B_{\mathrm{total}}(s,G,K) =Nglobal​Cstep=H​Ws2​G​log2​K.\displaystyle=N_{\mathrm{global}}\,C_{\mathrm{step}}=\tfrac{HW}{s^{2}}\,G\log_{2}K.

Here BtotalB_{\mathrm{total}} is a fixed-length nominal bit budget rather than the empirical entropy or effective semantic information of the learned codes.

The two variables control complementary properties. At fixed ss, increasing GG enlarges the representation capacity without increasing the number of global autoregressive steps. Increasing ss shortens the global sequence quadratically. These properties motivate spatial–group co-scaling: scaling ss by α\alpha and GG by α2\alpha^{2} preserves BtotalB_{\mathrm{total}} while reducing the number of global steps by a factor of α2\alpha^{2}.

Constructing the effective 64×64\times tokenizer.

Guided by this relation, we construct an effective 64×64\times tokenizer from the native 32×32\times tokenizer through the 2×22\times 2 spatial packing shown in Fig. 2(a). Each neighborhood of four quantized positions is packed into one global unit, increasing the codes per step from GqG_{q} to 4​Gq4G_{q} while shortening the global sequence by a factor of four. This realizes the co-scaling relation with α=2\alpha=2, preserving all quantized codes without introducing additional quantization. The packed codes are restored to the native grid before image decoding.

To validate this capacity analysis, we systematically vary the group size and evaluate reconstruction fidelity, semantic representation, and downstream generation in Sec. 5.2.1. The results confirm that increasing group size provides additional usable information capacity and improves representation quality. Larger code tuples, however, also increase the cost of intra-group dependency modeling, motivating the efficient depth decoder introduced next.

4.3 Efficient Intra-Group Modeling

Group scaling requires each global autoregressive step to generate a tuple of correlated discrete codes. A common approach, following RQ-Transformer [28], is to use a causal depth head to model intra-group dependencies, but its sequential decoding incurs increasing inference latency as the group size grows. Fully parallel prediction removes this serial overhead, yet sacrifices generation quality by ignoring these dependencies. To reconcile these competing objectives, we propose a semi-autoregressive head that preserves causal dependency modeling while approaching the decoding speed of parallel prediction. Below, we first examine the causal and parallel alternatives, then present our design.

At global decoding step tt, the autoregressive backbone produces a context representation 𝐡t\mathbf{h}_{t}. The intra-group head uses this context to generate GG codes, 𝐲t=(yt,1,…,yt,G)\mathbf{y}_{t}=(y_{t,1},\ldots,y_{t,G}), by modeling the conditional joint distribution p⁡(𝐲t∣𝐡t)p(\mathbf{y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t}).

Causal Autoregressive Head.

Following the spatial–depth decomposition of RQ-Transformer and its use in grouped-code generation [28, 36], a causal autoregressive head predicts the codes one by one, conditioning each prediction on the global context and previously generated codes:

pAR​(𝐲t∣𝐡t)=∏g=1Gp⁡(yt,g∣𝐡t,𝐲t,<g).p_{\mathrm{AR}}(\mathbf{y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t})=\prod_{g=1}^{G}p(y_{t,g}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t},\mathbf{y}_{t,<g}). (4)

This factorization preserves intra-group dependencies, but requires running the full head for each of the GG sequential predictions. As GG grows, this serial computation becomes a substantial decoding bottleneck and can dominate the global backbone under aggressive compression.

Parallel Prediction Head.

To remove this sequential overhead, a fully parallel head predicts all GG codes in a single forward pass:

pPAR​(𝐲t∣𝐡t)=∏g=1Gp⁡(yt,g∣𝐡t).p_{\mathrm{PAR}}(\mathbf{y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t})=\prod_{g=1}^{G}p(y_{t,g}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t}). (5)

This removes the intra-group serial path [4, 51, 40, 31], but makes the codes conditionally independent during sampling. Since codes within a group jointly describe the same visual content, independently sampled marginals may select incompatible modes, leading to multimodal collision [12]. The quality degradation motivates a head that retains causal conditioning while keeping most computation parallel.

Semi-Autoregressive Head.

We propose a semi-autoregressive head that combines a parallel trunk with a lightweight causal module, retaining intra-group dependencies without repeating expensive representation modeling GG times. Drawing architectural inspiration from the parallel–sequential drafters in DFlash and DSpark [5, 12], the parallel trunk first computes representations for all group slots in one pass:

𝐛t,1:G=Pψ([Mask]1:G;𝐡t).\mathbf{b}_{t,1:G}=P_{\psi}([\textsc{Mask}]_{1:G};\mathbf{h}_{t}). (6)

A lightweight, single-layer causal Transformer then generates each code conditioned on both its parallel representation and the previously sampled intra-group codes:

pSAR​(𝐲t∣𝐡t)=∏g=1Gp⁡(yt,g∣𝐡t,𝐛t,g,𝐲t,<g).p_{\mathrm{SAR}}(\mathbf{y}_{t}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t})=\prod_{g=1}^{G}p(y_{t,g}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t},\mathbf{b}_{t,g},\mathbf{y}_{t,<g}). (7)

The parallel trunk is evaluated only once per global position. Only the single-layer, KV-cached causal Transformer remains sequential, allowing each code to depend on previously sampled codes without repeatedly executing the full head. Experiments in Sec. 5.2.2 show that our head achieves generation quality comparable to the fully causal head with latency close to parallel prediction, while consistently outperforming the parallel head across all three quality metrics.

5 Experiments

Experimental setup.

We develop two models: GSTAR-Pro-8B, which uses a 32×32\times tokenizer with group size G=16G=16, and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B, which uses an effective 64×64\times tokenizer with G=32G=32 for fast image generation. Following prior progressive-training recipes [14, 7, 6], both models are trained through pretraining, continued training (CT), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT), with progressively increasing image resolution.Detailed tokenizer training procedures and stage-wise generator training configurations are provided in Appendix A. Both models support image generation and editing, evaluated in Sec. 5.1. We further analyze the effects of group scaling on reconstruction, generation, and semantic understanding in Sec. 5.2.1, compare the quality and latency of different prediction heads in Sec. 5.2.2, and investigate the sources of acceleration in Sec. 5.3.

5.1 Main Results

We adopt GenEval [20], DPG-Bench [23], PRISM [17], LongText-Bench [19], and Qwen-Image-Bench [30] to evaluate text-to-image generation, covering compositional alignment, perceptual quality, text rendering, and broader prompt-following capabilities. We evaluate instruction-guided image editing on GEdit-Bench [32], reporting semantic consistency, perceptual quality, and overall scores for its English subset. Results for GSTAR-Pro-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B are reported in Tables 1 and 5, respectively for generation and editing. Benchmark versions, sampling configurations, and evaluation protocols are detailed in Appendix C. We also evaluate the reconstruction quality of our visual tokenizers in Appendix E.

5.2 Ablation Studies

5.2.1 Group Scaling

We vary the group size G∈{1,8,16,32}G\in\{1,8,16,32\} while fixing the codebook size at K=16,384K=16{,}384 and the spatial compression factor at 32×32\times, and examine how increased per-position capacity affects reconstruction, generative modeling, and semantic understanding. Training details for the ImageNet ablations are provided in Appendix A.3. Generally, increasing GG improves reconstruction and semantic representation (Table 2), but slows early-stage generation convergence, consistent with VA-VAE [55]. Suprisingly, G=16G=16 eventually catches up with and outperforms G=8G=8, despite converging more slowly at first (Fig. 5).

We further validate this observation on text-to-image generation using the same setting as the head ablation in Sec. 5.2.2: Qwen3-1.7B initialization, a 32×32\times tokenizer, 100k pretraining steps at 512×512512\times 512 resolution, a sequence length of 8,192, and a global batch size of 32, followed by one epoch of SFT. Table 3 shows that G=16G=16 achieves comparable or slightly better performance.

Together with the late-stage ImageNet results, these findings suggest that larger groups provide a richer representational space that preserves more visual and semantic information. Although the resulting space is more difficult to model and leads to slower early-stage convergence, sufficient training allows the generator to exploit its increased capacity. Larger models may benefit even further from this additional capacity.

We also validate that our lossless packing strategy, which transforms f32g8\mathrm{f32g8} into f64g32\mathrm{f64g32}, retains strong text-to-image generation performance; see Appendix D.

5.2.2 Intra-Group Prediction Heads

We compare the Causal AR Head, Parallel Prediction Head, and our Semi-AR Head using a Qwen3-1.7B-initialized model with a 32×32\times tokenizer and G=16G=16. All variants share the same training setting: 100k pretraining steps at a fixed 512×512512\times 512 resolution, a sequence length of 8,192, and a global batch size of 32, followed by one epoch of SFT.

As shown in Table 5, our Semi-AR Head substantially reduces inference latency while maintaining generation quality comparable to the Causal AR Head. It also consistently outperforms the Parallel Prediction Head across all three quality metrics.

5.3 Efficiency Analysis

Our framework enables highly compressed visual representations that shorten the global autoregressive sequence, while the Semi-AR Head reduces the latency of intra-group modeling. Together, these designs reduce decoding costs at both the global and local levels. Beyond the architectural savings, we further optimize the system-level inference pipeline. We measure per-image latency for GSTAR-Flash-1.7B generating at 1024×10241024\times 1024 and apply four cumulative optimizations (Figure 5). Starting from a Causal AR head baseline of 22.23 s, replacing it with our Semi-AR Head reduces latency to 14.93 s (1.49×1.49\times) by parallelizing intra-group token prediction. The remaining optimizations target the two main bottlenecks separately: the intra-group head and the LLM backbone. For the head, we first capture each global step as a single CUDA graph, eliminating kernel-dispatch overhead (2.55×2.55\times, 5.85 s). We then fuse chains of small elementwise and reduction kernels in the sampling and normalization paths into composite Triton kernels, reducing the per-block kernel count and eliminating redundant global-memory round trips (1.74×1.74\times, 3.37 s). Finally, integrating the model into SGLang [62] for LLM backbone serving yields a further 1.35×1.35\times speedup (2.50 s). The four stages compound to an 8.9×8.9\times end-to-end speedup.

6 Conclusion

We explore high-quality autoregressive image generation under deep spatial compression by scaling discrete token capacity. Combining grouped quantization with efficient semi-autoregressive intra-group modeling enables generation at 32×32\times and 64×64\times spatial downsampling. Our GSTAR-Pro-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B models demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in large-scale text-to-image generation, achieving performance competitive with leading models and a 20×20\times speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models.

Appendix A Training Details

A.1 Model Training

Initialization and optimization.

We initialize GSTAR-Pro-8B from Qwen3-8B and GSTAR-Flash-1.7B from Qwen3-1.7B. Both models share the same three-stage training schedule, consisting of pretraining (PT), continued training (CT), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We use ZeRO Stage 2 throughout all three stages and optimize both models using Adam with β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 and β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95.

Training schedule.

We use any-resolution training throughout all three stages, progressively increasing the image resolution. PT runs for 400k steps at 512px, followed by 100k CT steps at 1024px. Both stages use a sequence length of 4,096, a global batch size of 64, and a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}. SFT runs for 30k steps, mixing 1024px and 2048px images at a ratio of 1:1, with a sequence length of 8,192, a global batch size of 32, and a learning rate of 10−510^{-5}. During SFT, image-editing and text-to-image generation data are mixed at a ratio of 3:7. Table 6 summarizes the configurations shared by both models.

Training data.

For PT and CT, we collect image–text pairs from publicly available datasets, including LAION, DataComp, and JourneyDB, and regenerate their captions using Qwen3.5-122B-A10B. For SFT, we select a higher-quality subset of these data and supplement it with a small proportion of images regenerated using Seedream and Nano Banana 2.

A.2 Tokenizer Training

Initialization and objectives.

We initialize the tokenizer encoder from Qwen-ViT with a spatial downsampling factor of 3232. For both the ImageNet ablations and text-to-image tokenizers, we use the same loss weights: λsem=1\lambda_{\mathrm{sem}}=1, λgram=10\lambda_{\mathrm{gram}}=10, λperceptual=1\lambda_{\mathrm{perceptual}}=1, λvq=1\lambda_{\mathrm{vq}}=1, and λcommit=0.25\lambda_{\mathrm{commit}}=0.25. Here λperceptual\lambda_{\mathrm{perceptual}} weights the perceptual reconstruction loss, and λcommit\lambda_{\mathrm{commit}} weights the commitment term within the vector-quantization objective.

Optimization.

All tokenizers are trained with Adam using (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) and a global batch size of 1,024. We use a base learning rate of 10−410^{-4} for the quantizer, decoder, and other components. To preserve the pretrained semantic encoder’s semantic representations, we use a lower learning rate of 10−510^{-5} for the encoder.

Tokenizer configurations.

For GSTAR-Pro-8B, we train a 32×32\times tokenizer with 16 quantization groups per spatial position. For GSTAR-Flash-1.7B, we train a 32×32\times tokenizer with 8 quantization groups per spatial position, then merge each 2×22\times 2 neighborhood of quantized positions to obtain an effective 64×64\times tokenizer with 32 groups per global position. This merging operation reorganizes the quantized representation without introducing an additional quantization step.

Tokenizers for text-to-image generation.

We use any-resolution training for the text-to-image tokenizers. In addition to general-purpose image data, we incorporate OCR, aesthetic, and face data to improve generalization and text-rendering capabilities. Training runs for a total of 200k steps.

Following UniAR [42] and Emu3.5 [13], we freeze the tokenizer after training and train a DiT-based visual decoder initialized from Ideogram 4 [25], conditioned on the discrete tokens produced by the frozen tokenizer. This decoder is used solely to refine visual quality. Unlike GLM-Image [59] and X-Omni [19], our decoder conditions exclusively on our discrete visual tokens, without any additional textual conditioning. The ImageNet ablation settings are described separately in Appendix A.3.

A.3 ImageNet Ablation Settings

Tokenizer training.

For the ImageNet ablations, we train the tokenizers on ImageNet for 100k steps at a fixed resolution of 256×256256\times 256. The loss weights, optimizer, component-wise learning rates, and global batch size follow Appendix A.2.

Class-conditional generation.

For the class-to-image (C2I) ablations, we train the autoregressive generator on ImageNet at 256×256256\times 256 resolution using the Llama-XL architecture from LlamaGen [46]. We train for 50k steps with a sequence length of 4,096, a global batch size of 128, and a learning rate of 4×10−44\times 10^{-4}. All remaining hyperparameters follow the Llama-XL configuration.

Appendix B Multimodal Understanding

Experimental setup.

We initialize the language model from Qwen3-1.7B and train on the standard LLaVA-OneVision training data [29]. We compare continuous visual representations from the original Qwen3 ViT (without further training) with discrete representations produced by our f32g16 tokenizer, which uses a spatial downsampling factor of 3232 and 1616 quantization groups per position.

Results.

As shown in Table 7, our discrete tokenizer achieves multimodal understanding performance comparable to continuous visual representations, with average scores of 64.7 and 64.6, respectively. These results suggest that our tokenizer largely preserves the semantic information needed for multimodal understanding despite discretization and spatial compression.

Appendix C Evaluation Protocols and Additional Results

C.1 Latency Measurement

We measure batch-one generation at 1024×10241024\times 1024 on an NVIDIA H200 and separately report global-backbone time, total intra-group head time, image-decoder time, and end-to-end pipeline latency. All models run in BF16 precision. The software stack consists of PyTorch 2.9.1 with CUDA 12.8, Triton 3.5.1, and Transformers 4.57.6. The decode loop is captured as a single CUDA graph. Each configuration is warmed up for 3 iterations, then timed over 3 independent trials; we report the median latency. Sampling uses classifier-free guidance with a scale of 1.8, temperature 0.5, and top-kk = 1024. We report run-to-run variation with the final measurements. Matched comparisons use identical timing boundaries and implementation settings.

Appendix D Lossless Packing at 64×64\times Spatial Compression

We evaluate whether our lossless packing strategy can increase the spatial compression factor while preserving both tokenizer reconstruction and text-to-image generation performance. Starting from f32g8\mathrm{f32g8} (i.e., 32×32\times spatial compression with G=8G=8; other configurations follow the same notation), we pack each 2×22\times 2 neighborhood of spatial latent positions along the group dimension to obtain f64g32\mathrm{f64g32}. Specifically, four spatial positions with eight groups each are rearranged into a single spatial position with 32 groups. This operation is exactly invertible and neither discards nor re-quantizes any latent codes. Consequently, applying the inverse packing operation before decoding yields identical tokenizer reconstruction by construction, while reducing the number of spatial latent positions by 4×4\times.

To assess the effect of packing on generation, we train the text-to-image generator with the f64g32\mathrm{f64g32} representation using the same training recipe as for the f32g8\mathrm{f32g8} baseline. The results are reported in Table 8.

As shown in Table 8, the packed f64g32\mathrm{f64g32} representation achieves a GenEval score of 0.7885, a DPG score of 80.44, and a PRISM score of 5.13. Compared with f32g8\mathrm{f32g8}, it retains strong generative performance despite using a 4×4\times shorter spatial latent sequence. These results demonstrate that our lossless packing strategy enables effective text-to-image generation at a 64×64\times spatial compression factor without altering the reconstruction capability of the tokenizer.

Appendix E Image Reconstruction Quality

We also evaluate the reconstruction capability of our visual tokenizers on the ImageNet validation set at a fixed resolution of 512×512512\times 512. We report peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and compare against five open-source visual tokenizers: VQGAN [16], IBQ [44], VAR [47], Open-MAGVIT2 [35], and Emu3.5 [13].

As shown in Table 9, our f32g16 tokenizer achieves the highest PSNR of 25.12 dB at 32×32\times effective spatial compression, exceeding Open-MAGVIT2 by 1.14 dB. At 64×64\times effective spatial compression, our f64g32 variant achieves 23.90 dB, outperforming VQGAN, IBQ, VAR, and Emu3.5 while remaining within 0.08 dB of Open-MAGVIT2. These results show that our tokenizers retain competitive reconstruction fidelity at substantially higher effective spatial compression factors.

We also present qualitative reconstruction examples in Figure 6, comparing the ViT decoder and the refiner for both the f32g16 and f64g32 tokenizers. The examples illustrate how the refiner improves visual detail and sharpness while preserving the overall image content.
